content:
This section, spanning file pages 239 through 243 (printed labels 408 through 416 visible), turns from cognition to social strategy and emotion. Steven Pinker opens with nuclear deterrence and the Doomsday Machine from *Dr. Strangelove*: an automatic, irrevocable retaliation system works only if its existence is announced, because deterrence depends on the enemy's certainty (file page 239). He generalizes via Thomas Schelling: in strategic conflicts where interests partly compete and partly overlap, ordinary assets—intelligence, options, communication, rationality, self-interest—can become liabilities, since behavior is calculated by predicting the other party's counter-response (file pages 239–240).

Bargaining illustrates recursive prediction: each side guesses what the other will concede, and any price in the acceptable range is one someone would have backed off from (file page 240). The winning tactic is "a voluntary but irreversible sacrifice of freedom of choice"—a public enforceable bet capping one's price, a salesperson without discount authority, a mortgage blocked by appraisal (file page 240). Promises work similarly: being bound makes them credible, which is why the right to be sued enables contracts, and foreclosure law paradoxically helps borrowers (file page 240). Threats that are costly to carry out are credible only when the threatener has no choice—hence the steering wheel thrown away, the hijacker's jostle-triggered explosives, or the appearance of irrationality (bloodshot eyes, suicide bombers) (file pages 240–241). Defenses likewise involve self-incapacitation: incommunicado kidnappers, burned bridges, "driver does not know combination to safe" (file page 241). These paradoxes can escalate into cycles of mutual self-binding, as in protesters handcuffed to tracks versus a nearsighted engineer (file pages 241–242).

Pinker's central claim about emotion follows: strong passions function like physical handcuffs. Shame, rage, or honor make one's commitments credible because they are involuntary and unresponsive to cost (file page 242). He inverts the Romantic view—passions are not the enemy of reason but guarantors of its bargains, promises, and threats; the intellect deliberately relinquishes control to them (file pages 241–242). The Falklands War, revenge, and honor are cited as costly commitments whose deterrent value requires publicity; vengeance persists even where law makes it obsolete (file page 242). Because a doomsday machine must be advertised, emotions are displayed on the face (file page 242). Pinker notes Darwin's own theory of expression was Lamarckian, and criticizes a blood-flow hypothesis as hydraulically implausible and unable to explain audience effects (file page 242).

Sham emotions create a problem: fakers would prosper, yet genuine expressions survive because they are hard to fake—social smiles use different muscles than involuntary pleasure smiles (file page 243). Pinker admits the explanation is incomplete: he does not know why voluntary control never evolved, and points to costly-signaling theory (the peacock's tail) as a possible answer (file page 243). His own guess is that natural selection segregated voluntary cognition from housekeeping physiology (heartbeat, sweating), handcuffing each emotion to involuntary circuits whose visible effects—flushing, trembling, weeping—serve as honest signals, much as the Soviets would display the Doomsday Machine's wiring (file page 243). He flags this as unproven, though the vigilance for sham emotions is undeniable (file page 243). The text ends mid-sentence about telecommunications; the remainder is absent.

Engineering implications, kept separate: the section offers no primitive operations for perception, compositionality, or learning. It does suggest design principles for a social reasoning module: represent recursive beliefs about others' predictions (bargaining), model commitments as constraints on future action (promises, threats), and treat involuntary signals as costly credentials. A thinking machine would need explicit representations of agents, their goals, and counterfactual choices—plus a way to distinguish permitted scope of a rule (a credible threat's trigger conditions) from mere memorized cases. Innate versus acquired is not addressed here; the emotion theory is evolutionary speculation, not a learning law. Nothing in this section demonstrates general intelligence or consciousness.
